assumptions: Outcome thresholds can be specified without making the customer responsible for opaque or unobservable exclusions.
Homeowners can grant lawful access to the necessary meter, indoor-temperature, installation, device, weather, and service-event data.
Any regulated risk is carried by an authorized partner and the venture initially provides measurement and administration rather than unauthorized insurance.
Installer-delivered remediation can be contracted separately from independent performance measurement.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Paid pilot commitments from installers or owners; a preregistered weather-adjusted performance definition; a season of consented site-level telemetry linked to diagnoses and remedies; measured dispute reduction or energy savings; delivery cost and retention data; and written carrier and regulatory feedback on a compliant risk-bearing structure.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Turning a heat-pump sale from an equipment promise into a measured comfort or efficiency outcome addresses a real accountability gap across design, installation, controls, weather, and service. The central metric is difficult to attribute fairly, however, and the candidate has not shown that an independent performance promise is preferable to monitoring, maintenance, or an ordinary equipment warranty.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Unexpected energy use, comfort misses, and post-install disputes can impose meaningful costs on owners and installers. The proposed recurring cover fee, loss frequency, buyer, and purchase decision are unevidenced, while existing equipment warranties reduce perceived incremental value and installers may resist a product that formalizes disputes.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Separating a monitoring and administration fee from carrier-held risk is more disciplined than self-underwriting and could yield recurring revenue. Neither claims frequency nor attribution error, remediation cost, carrier share, telemetry cost, adverse selection, reserve needs, or acquisition cost is measured, so the stated margins and payback cannot yet be relied upon.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Heat pumps are a mature, policy-supported technology with a growing long-lived installed base, and a consenting installer cohort offers a plausible pilot. The candidate does not size a segment with compatible telemetry, sufficiently homogeneous buildings, repeated performance complaints, and a budget for third-party outcome cover.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Vendor-neutral measurement and auditable thresholds could be useful when responsibility is fragmented. OEMs and large installers control diagnostics, warranty interpretation, and the original customer relationship and can add monitoring or extended service cheaply, while insurers can demand broader data and contractual controls.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A validated measurement and risk-administration system could extend across installer portfolios, property managers, equipment brands, and adjacent building-performance outcomes. Expansion increases heterogeneity in envelopes, occupancy, tariffs, climates, controls, and service quality, which can weaken rather than automatically improve underwriting.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Consented longitudinal links among design, weather, controls, service actions, comfort, and energy could eventually support proprietary benchmarks and better risk selection. Data access is currently uncontracted and may be controlled or revoked by homeowners, installers, and device vendors; the proposed cover and thresholds can be copied by better-positioned incumbents.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The founder's analytical skills and a family installer route help create a small lawful measurement pilot. They provide no present source-data rights, customer contract, service authority, claims history, actuarial capability, or carrier agreement, so the most valuable resources remain external.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: EU decarbonization and building-renovation policy support continuing heat-pump deployment, increasing the future population of systems requiring performance oversight. Heat pumps are already mature technology, so policy momentum alone does not create urgency for a new warranty category or remove the evidence burden around outcomes.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Attaching enrollment to installation or annual service is operationally coherent and could make acquisition efficient. The installer owns the initial relationship and may see independent scoring as liability rather than sales enablement; no installer commitment, attachment rate, or direct customer retention has been demonstrated.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The venture must normalize building and occupant effects, secure multi-party data, detect performance misses, coordinate field remediation, draft consumer-safe promises, and stay within insurance regulation while depending on an authorized carrier for risk. These coupled requirements are unusually demanding for a part-time, low-capital launch despite the possibility of beginning with monitoring only.

highest_value_structural_change: Remove risk transfer from the initial offer and sell an installer-funded, season-long measurement and root-cause protocol with tightly bounded system classes, converting to carrier-backed cover only after observed miss frequency and remediation cost make the outcome actuarially legible.
main_structural_strength: The concept aligns payment with a measurable operating outcome rather than merely selling equipment, and a cross-brand evidence layer could clarify responsibility among owners, installers, OEMs, and risk carriers.
primary_score_limiter: The insured or guaranteed outcome is not yet shown to be measurable, attributable, desired, or economically priceable, and every essential data, service, distribution, and risk-capital agreement remains hypothetical.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Modern systems already have equipment warranties, and building-envelope quality plus occupant behavior can dominate comfort and energy use; this combination both weakens incremental willingness to pay and makes a simple performance promise vulnerable to frequent disputes or exclusions.
